pages.title: Overview
pages.body:
Dust & Blood

A traditional Western tabletop roleplaying game about hard choices, difficult journeys, and the lives people build on the frontier.

This reference organizes the rules text currently available in this conversation into a clean, searchable handbook. Use the sidebar to browse sections or search for a term from the rules.

Compilation note: This edition includes the complete rules text provided in chat and the additional general rules already discussed. The FilePaste link’s full contents were not retrievable here, so sections whose detailed source text has not been provided are marked as needing the manuscript text.

Quick Reference

RuleValue
Core ScoresMight, Agility, Condition, Intelligence, Wisdom, Charisma
Starting Proficiency Bonus+2
Starting Health10 + Condition score
Action Points refreshed3 at the start of your active turn
Saved AP maximum12
Foot movement1 AP per 5 feet
Default Reputation0, unless modified by Background or Flaw
Trait Rank IIIAvailable from Level 5

Classless Character Design

Characters are shaped by Backgrounds, Proficiencies, Traits, Flaws, equipment, and choices in play rather than by traditional classes. A character might develop into a scout, mounted traveler, brawler, field medic, or another archetype through their investments.

pages.title: Core Scores & Health
pages.body:
Core Scores & Health

Every character has six Core Scores. Add the corresponding modifier to d20 rolls that use that score.

The Six Core Scores

ScoreMeaning
MightPhysical power and strength.
AgilitySpeed, coordination, reflexes, and precision.
ConditionPhysical toughness and endurance.
IntelligenceReasoning, knowledge, education, and problem-solving.
WisdomPerception, judgment, instincts, and awareness.
CharismaPersonality, influence, confidence, and social ability.

Rolling Core Scores

  1. Roll 4d6 for one score.
  2. Discard the lowest die and add the remaining three dice.
  3. Repeat six times.
  4. Assign the six results to your Core Scores in any order.

Core Score Modifiers

ScoreModifier
1−5
2–3−4
4–5−3
6–7−2
8–9−1
10–11+0
12–13+1
14–15+2
16–17+3
18+4

Health

At character creation, starting Health is 10 + your Condition score. Each time your character gains a level, they gain an additional 1d6 Health, unless a Trait or another ability changes how Health is gained.

Defense Bonus (DB)

Your Defense Bonus is determined by the Defense Points (DP) provided by equipped clothing. Add the DP of each equipped clothing item together to determine your DB.

Example: A traveler’s shirt provides 7 DP, pants provide 5 DP, and a hat provides 2 DP. Together, they provide DB 14.

pages.title: Proficiencies
pages.body:
Proficiencies

Proficiency represents training or specialized experience in a skill, tool, weapon, or saving throw.

Using Proficiency

When you attempt an action you are proficient in, add your Proficiency Bonus (PB) to the roll alongside the relevant Core Score modifier. For example, a Ranch Hand proficient in Animal Handling adds PB to checks involving handling or calming animals.

A character without the relevant proficiency still makes the check using the appropriate Core Score modifier, unless a specific rule says otherwise.

Proficiency Bonus

All characters begin with PB +2. The bonus represents overall experience and increases with progression; it is not determined by how many proficiencies a character has.

Important: Add PB only once per roll, even if more than one proficiency applies, unless a specific rule states otherwise.

Types of Proficiency

Proficiencies can cover skills, tools, weapons, or saving throws. Backgrounds grant the proficiencies listed in their entries. Other proficiencies may be developed through character advancement where permitted by the rules.

pages.title: Checks & Saves
pages.body:
Checks & Saves

Use a Core Score check when the outcome of an attempted action is uncertain and the result matters.

Making a Check

Roll a d20 and add the relevant Core Score modifier. If the character is proficient in the applicable skill or activity, add PB once. The Game Master determines the appropriate score and whether proficiency applies.

Difficulty Classes

When a rule gives a Difficulty Class (DC), the check succeeds if the total meets or exceeds that DC. Some specific rules call for a saving throw or another opposed check instead.

Playtest note: Use the exact DC and check type stated by the individual rule. The full general DC ladder was not included in the text shared here.

pages.title: Character Creation
pages.body:
Character Creation

Build a character through ability scores, Background, equipment, Traits, and Flaws.

Creation Steps

  1. Roll six Core Scores using 4d6, dropping the lowest die each time, then assign the results in any order.
  2. Calculate the modifier for each Core Score.
  3. Choose a Background and record its Proficiencies, capabilities, drawbacks, and any starting Reputation or debt.
  4. Choose the Background starting kit or starting money.
  5. Calculate starting Health as 10 + Condition.
  6. Calculate DB from the Defense Points of equipped clothing.
  7. Record starting PB +2.
  8. Choose Traits and Flaws using the Character Point rules supplied by the game.
  9. Record alignment if required by the chosen Background.

Character Points

Dust & Blood uses a classless Trait and Flaw system. Traits cost CP and may have multiple ranks; Flaws grant CP in exchange for meaningful disadvantages. Additional CP gained at later levels can be spent on character options allowed by the rules.

Trait Rank Limits

Ranks must be purchased in order: Rank I before Rank II, and Rank II before Rank III. At Level 1, only Trait Ranks I and II are available. Rank III becomes available at Level 5.

Meaningful Trade-offs

Some Traits may cap or limit other Traits. For example, the supplied draft gives Sprinter II as an example that might cap Sneak at Rank I. These limits encourage specialization rather than allowing every character to master everything.

pages.title: Backgrounds
pages.body:
Backgrounds

A Background represents the occupation, upbringing, or way of life that shaped a character before the game began.

Ranch Hand

Has spent significant time working with livestock and horses.

Proficiencies: Animal Handling, Riding.

Capability: Hard Worker (+2 Might).

Cons: Rough Hands (−3 Agility); Lost Opportunity (−2 Intelligence).

Starting money: $10. Kit: Work clothes, bedroll, canteen, rope, work knife, saddle, bridle.

Blacksmith

Has trained in working and shaping metal.

Proficiencies: Blacksmithing, Metalworking.

Cons: Rough Hands (−3 Agility); Socially Weird (−1 Charisma).

Starting money: $25. Kit: Work clothes, apron, blacksmith hammer, tongs, small tool kit, whetstone.

Lawman

The supplied heading says “Lawyer,” but the description and kit refer to a Lawman; this reference uses Lawman.

Proficiencies: Investigation, Intimidation.

Capability: +5 starting Reputation.

Restriction: Must have Lawful alignment.

Starting money: $30. Kit: Lawman’s badge, uniform or coat, handcuffs, notebook, writing supplies, watch.

Gambler

Has spent significant time playing games of chance.

Proficiencies: Gambling, Deception.

Cons: Owes $20 in starting debt.

Starting money: $15. Kit: Decent clothes, deck of cards, dice, small notebook, flask.

Outlaw

Has survived outside the protection of lawful society.

Proficiencies: Stealth, Survival.

Cons: Wanted Man; starting Reputation −5.

Starting money: $5. Kit: Worn clothes, bedroll, canteen, rope, knife, lockpicks.

Doctor

Has received formal medical training.

Proficiencies: Medicine, Herbalism.

Cons: Pacifist; disadvantage on firearm attacks.

Starting money: $75. Kit: Doctor’s bag, medical tools, bandages, antiseptic, surgical knife, notebook, watch.

Starting Money

BackgroundMoneyReason supplied
Ranch Hand$10Low-paid work, often partly compensated with food or lodging.
Blacksmith$25Skilled trade with higher wages.
Lawman$30Stable paid position.
Gambler$15Unstable income.
Outlaw$5Constantly moving makes saving difficult.
Doctor$75Highly skilled professional.

Levels & Experience

Characters earn XP by completing jobs, overcoming challenges, and accomplishing objectives.

Characters begin at Level 1 with 0 XP. The XP column is the total accumulated XP needed to reach a level, not the amount needed since the previous level. The CP reward is granted once upon reaching that level.

Spending CP

CP can be invested in new Traits, higher Trait ranks, Ability Score Improvements, Feats, Knowledge, proficiencies, and specialized abilities where those options are available. Exact CP costs belong to the relevant option entry.

pages.title: Reputation
pages.body:
Reputation

Reputation tracks how NPCs perceive and respond to a character. It represents public perception, not necessarily the truth about a character.

Range

Reputation ranges from −20 to +20. Characters normally start at 0 unless a Background or Flaw changes it. An Outlaw starts at −5.

Negative Reputation

As Reputation becomes more negative, NPCs may become suspicious, hostile, or unwilling to associate with the character. They might refuse service, deny help, or alert authorities.

At −20, a character is likely notorious nationwide for extraordinarily infamous actions. Reaching that level requires extreme notoriety; ordinary crimes and everyday misbehavior are not enough.

Positive Reputation

As Reputation becomes more positive, NPCs are increasingly likely to trust, respect, and assist the character. High Reputation may provide better deals, opportunities, and cooperation. At +20, a character is exceptionally respected and may be famous nationwide for extraordinary deeds.

Changing Reputation

Reputation changes through actions, accomplishments, and what other people learn about the character. The Game Master decides how widely events are known and how they affect public standing.

pages.title: Action Points & Turns
pages.body:
Action Points & Turns

Action Points (AP) represent a character’s capacity to act during a combat round.

Regaining AP

  • At the start of your active turn, regenerate 3 AP.
  • You may save unused AP, up to a maximum of 12 saved AP.

Movement

Moving on foot costs 1 AP per 5 feet.

Live Combat

Under the Live Combat rule, saved AP can be spent on an inactive turn to move, take cover, reload, or interact. Saved AP cannot be used to make firearm attacks during another character’s turn.

Actions and turns

Specific action costs and combat resolution depend on the individual action rules. Use the relevant entry in the full manuscript for details not included in the text available here.

pages.title: Mounts
pages.body:
Mounts

Mounts are a big part of Dust & Blood, but live mounts such as oxen and horses require their own sheet.

Horses

1. Horse Creation

Create a horse using these steps:

  1. Choose a breed and apply its attribute bonuses.
  2. Roll 1d6 for individual quality.
  3. Choose or roll its temperament.
  4. Calculate HP, DB, speed, stamina, and carrying capacity.
  5. Choose its training.
  6. Record its identification, equipment, and price.

Horses use the same six attributes and modifiers as characters: Might, Agility, Condition, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma.

Individual Quality

Roll 1d6 after applying breed bonuses.

RollEffect
1Primary attribute -1
2Secondary attribute -1
3–4No change
5Primary attribute +1
6Primary attribute +1 and secondary attribute +1

The GM determines which attributes are primary and secondary for each breed. This roll can change each attribute by no more than 1.

2. Horse Breeds

BreedAttribute BonusesSpecialization
Quarter HorseMight +1, Agility +1, Condition +1Ranch work
ThoroughbredAgility +2, Condition +1Speed and pursuit
Paint HorseAgility +1, Condition +1, Wisdom +1General riding and stock work
SaddlebredAgility +2, Charisma +1Responsive riding
Draft HorseMight +2, Condition +2, Wisdom +1Heavy hauling

Breed bonuses represent natural abilities, not training.

3. Horse Statistics

Hit Points (HP)

HP = 10 + Condition modifier + Breed HP bonus

Horse TypeHP Bonus
Light riding horse+0
Standard riding horse+2
Heavy riding horse+3
Draft horse+5

At 0 HP, a horse is incapacitated and cannot be ridden or work normally.

Defense Bonus (DB)

DB = 10 + Agility modifier + Armor DP

Armor DP comes from protective equipment; ordinary saddles and bridles provide none.

Speed

GaitBase Speed
Walking20 ft./round
Trotting30 ft./round
Cantering40 ft./round
Galloping60 ft./round
  • Thoroughbred: +10 ft. to cantering and galloping.
  • Draft horse: -10 ft. to cantering and galloping.
  • Other breeds: No change.

Extended fast travel may require stamina checks.

Stamina

  • Maximum Stamina: 6 + Condition modifier.
  • Strenuous travel or heavy labor: -1 Stamina per hour.
  • Galloping for a full minute: An additional -1 Stamina.
  • At 0 Stamina: Cannot gallop and suffers -2 to physical checks.
  • Rest: Recover 2 Stamina per hour with water and reasonable conditions.
  • Full night's rest: Restore all Stamina with adequate food, water, and shelter.

The GM may adjust costs for terrain, weather, workload, and condition.

Carrying Capacity

Might ModifierComfortable Load
-1 or lower100 lb.
+0150 lb.
+1200 lb.
+2250 lb.
+3300 lb.
+4350 lb.

These are provisional game values, not real-world load recommendations. Smaller, injured, or exhausted horses may have lower limits.

Exceeding the comfortable load reduces speed by 10 ft. and costs an additional 1 Stamina per hour. A horse should not carry more than 150% of its comfortable load.

4. Temperament

TemperamentEffect
Calm+2 to remain steady around sudden noises and unfamiliar situations
Steady+1 to routine handling
Nervous-2 to remain calm around sudden threats
Stubborn-2 to accept unfamiliar commands
Spirited+2 to responsiveness and energetic movement; -1 to remain calm when frightened
Aggressive-2 to routine handling around unfamiliar people or animals

Apply modifiers only when relevant.

5. Training

TrainingCapability
UntrainedNo reliable riding or work training
RidingResponds to ordinary riding commands
Ranch WorkPerforms routine ranch tasks, including moving cattle
Pack HorseCarries supplies and follows a handler
War-TrainedTolerates combat noise and responds under battlefield pressure
RacingTrained for speed, pacing, and competition

A horse may have multiple training types with GM approval. Training does not eliminate fear, pain, or exhaustion.

6. Riding and Handling

When a task is difficult or dangerous, the GM may call for an Animal Handling check using the normal check rules.

TaskDifficulty
Mount a calm, trained horse5
Control ordinary travel8
Navigate difficult terrain10
Calm a frightened horse12
Ride through nearby gunfire15
Control an unfamiliar, panicking horse18
Perform an exceptional maneuver20

These are suggested difficulties. Failure does not automatically cause a fall; consequences depend on the situation.

  • Mounting: No check for a cooperative horse under normal conditions.
  • Dismounting: No check under normal conditions.
  • Riding armed: Difficult shots or riding at a gallop may require checks or penalties.
  • Falling: The GM may call for an Agility check to land safely; failure uses normal falling-damage rules.

Fear and Panic

Gunfire, predators, fires, injuries, and sudden threats may trigger a Wisdom-based check using the horse's Wisdom modifier.

On success, the horse remains under control. On failure, it may hesitate, flee, rear, or resist commands. Temperament, training, and threat severity affect the outcome. Appropriate combat training may grant a bonus against gunfire-related fear.

7. Injuries and Care

ConditionEffect
ExhaustedCannot gallop; -2 to physical checks
LimpingSpeed reduced by 10 ft.
IncapacitatedCannot be ridden or work normally
FrightenedMay flee or resist commands
SickMay suffer Condition-check and Stamina-recovery penalties

The GM determines injury severity, duration, and treatment. HP recovers through rest and appropriate care under the game's healing rules. Serious injuries may require veterinary knowledge or professional treatment.

Horses need regular food, water, rest, grooming, and appropriate hoof care. Neglect can cause sickness and impair recovery. The GM may handle routine care narratively unless survival or ranch management is central to the campaign.

8. Horse Equipment and Prices

ItemPricePurpose
Basic Horse$30Ordinary horse with minimal specialized training
Trained Horse$50Trained for one common activity

Prices are starting values in the game's dollar economy. Breed, age, condition, temperament, and training may change a horse's price. Equipment is purchased separately unless included in the sale.

10. Horse Core Rules

  • Horses use the same six attributes and modifier rules as characters.
  • Breed determines natural specialization; individual quality distinguishes horses of the same breed.
  • Temperament affects behavior, while training determines reliable capabilities.
  • HP, DB, speed, stamina, and carrying capacity determine physical performance.
  • Equipment is separate unless included in the purchase price.
  • The GM determines when checks are required and what failure means.
  • Horses can become frightened, exhausted, injured, or sick and require proper care.
  • All horse mechanics must remain compatible with the game's attributes, Action Points, combat, and equipment systems.

Oxen

1. Oxen Creation

Create an ox using these steps:

  1. Choose a breed and apply its attribute bonuses.
  2. Roll 1d6 for individual quality.
  3. Choose or roll its temperament.
  4. Calculate HP, DB, speed, stamina, and pulling capacity.
  5. Record its training, identification, equipment, and price.

Oxen use the same six attributes and modifiers as characters: Might, Agility, Condition, Intelligence, Wisdom, and Charisma.

Oxen are primarily working animals used for pulling wagons, plowing fields, and hauling heavy supplies. They can be trained to follow commands and work in teams but are not suitable for ordinary riding.

Individual Quality

Roll 1d6 after applying breed bonuses.

RollEffect
1Primary attribute -1
2Secondary attribute -1
3–4No change
5Primary attribute +1
6Primary attribute +1 and secondary attribute +1

The GM determines primary and secondary attributes for each breed. Each attribute can change by no more than 1 from this roll.

2. Ox Breeds

BreedAttribute BonusesSpecialization
HerefordMight +1, Condition +1General farm work
AngusCondition +2, Might +1Endurance and steady labor
Texas LonghornAgility +1, Wisdom +1Rough terrain and frontier conditions
CharolaisMight +2, Condition +1Heavy pulling
HighlandCondition +1, Wisdom +1Cold weather and rugged terrain

These are proposed game bonuses representing breed specialization. Oxen of other breeds can be added using the same system.

3. Ox Statistics

Hit Points (HP)

HP = 10 + Condition modifier + Size HP bonus

SizeHP Bonus
Small+0
Standard+3
Large+5

At 0 HP, an ox is incapacitated and cannot work normally.

Defense Bonus (DB)

DB = 10 + Agility modifier + Armor DP

Armor DP comes from protective equipment. Ordinary yokes and harnesses provide no armor.

Speed

MovementSpeed
Walking20 ft./round
Working Pace15 ft./round
Fast Walk25 ft./round

Oxen cannot gallop like horses. Their speed while pulling a load depends on the load, terrain, and condition of the animal.

Stamina

  • Maximum Stamina: 6 + Condition modifier.
  • Heavy labor: -1 Stamina per hour.
  • Sustained maximum-effort pulling: An additional -1 Stamina per hour.
  • At 0 Stamina: The ox becomes exhausted, cannot perform heavy pulling, and suffers -2 to physical checks.
  • Rest: Recover 2 Stamina per hour with water and reasonable conditions.
  • Full night's rest: Restore all Stamina with adequate food, water, and shelter.

The GM may adjust stamina costs for terrain, weather, and workload.

Pulling Capacity

Pulling capacity determines the weight an ox can move using a suitable yoke or harness. It represents the total load being pulled, not the weight carried on the animal's back.

Might ModifierComfortable Pulling Load
-1 or lower500 lb.
+0750 lb.
+11,000 lb.
+21,250 lb.
+31,500 lb.
+41,750 lb.

These are provisional game-balance values, not real-world hauling recommendations.

  • Difficult terrain, steep slopes, mud, and poor weather can reduce pulling capacity.
  • Loads above comfortable capacity require GM approval and increase Stamina expenditure.
  • An ox should not exceed 150% of its comfortable pulling capacity.
  • Two oxen working as a team can pull more than one, but their combined capacity depends on training, harnessing, and coordination.

4. Temperament

TemperamentEffect
Calm+2 to remain steady around sudden noises and unfamiliar situations
Steady+1 to routine handling
Nervous-2 to remain calm around sudden threats
Stubborn-2 to accept unfamiliar commands
Spirited+2 to responsiveness; -1 to remain calm when frightened
Aggressive-2 to routine handling around unfamiliar people or animals

Apply modifiers only when relevant.

5. Training

TrainingCapability
UntrainedNo reliable working commands
Draft WorkPulls carts and wagons using suitable harnesses
PlowingTrained to pull agricultural equipment
Team-TrainedWorks alongside another draft animal
Pack-TrainedAccepts a limited load and follows a handler
Road-TrainedPulls loads along established roads and routes

Training does not eliminate fear, pain, or exhaustion. Riding is not a standard capability.

6. Handling and Work Checks

The GM may call for an Animal Handling check when controlling an ox in difficult or dangerous circumstances.

TaskDifficulty
Lead a calm, trained ox5
Direct ordinary farm work8
Guide an ox through difficult terrain10
Calm a frightened ox12

These are suggested difficulties. Failure may cause an ox to stop, resist commands, change direction, or disrupt a team.

Fear and Panic

Gunfire, predators, fires, and sudden threats may trigger a Wisdom-based check using the ox's Wisdom modifier. On failure, the ox may hesitate, flee, or resist commands. Training and temperament influence the outcome.

7. Injuries and Care

ExhaustedCannot perform heavy pulling; -2 to physical checks
LimpingSpeed reduced by 10 ft.
IncapacitatedCannot work normally
FrightenedMay flee or resist commands
SickMay suffer Condition-check and Stamina-recovery penalties

The GM determines injury severity and treatment. HP recovers through rest and appropriate care under the game's healing rules. Serious injuries may require veterinary knowledge or professional treatment.

Oxen require regular food, water, rest, grooming, hoof care, and properly fitted yokes or harnesses. Neglect can cause sickness and impair recovery.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.body:
Rules Glossary

TermMeaning
APAction Points, used to pay for actions.
ASIAbility Score Improvement.
BackgroundAn occupation, upbringing, or way of life that shaped a character.
CPCharacter Points, used to purchase character options.
DBDefense Bonus, based on equipped clothing’s Defense Points.
DCDifficulty Class, the target number for a check or save.
DPDefense Points provided by clothing.
FlawA meaningful disadvantage that grants CP.
PBProficiency Bonus; all characters begin at +2.
ProficiencyTraining or specialized experience in a skill, tool, weapon, or saving throw.
ReputationA value from −20 to +20 representing public perception.
TraitA character option purchased with CP, sometimes with multiple ranks.
XPExperience Points used to determine level progression.

pages.title: Core Combat System
pages.body:
Core Combat System

Core Resolution

Dust & Blood uses a d20 as its primary resolution die. When a character attempts something with a meaningful chance of success or failure, the player rolls a d20 and applies the appropriate modifiers. This system keeps gameplay simple and fast while allowing combat, skills, and other mechanics to remain flexible.

Action Points (AP)

The game uses an Action Point system to determine how much a character can do. AP can be spent on movement, drawing or holstering weapons, reloading, taking cover, interacting with objects, climbing, and other actions. Characters can also save unused AP for later turns.

Turn Definitions

  • Active Turn: The turn currently belonging to your character.
  • Inactive Turn: Any turn belonging to another character.

AP Regeneration

At the start of each active turn, a player regenerates 3 AP. These AP are added to any AP the character has saved from previous turns; saved AP are not lost when new AP are gained. For example, if a character has 3 AP saved when their next active turn begins, they will have 6 AP available. The absolute most a character can have at any given time is 12 AP.

Characters regenerate AP even while unconscious. However, regenerating AP does not necessarily mean an unconscious character can spend those AP to perform actions.

Live Combat

Live Combat allows characters to spend their available AP outside their active turns. During a friend's turn or an enemy's turn, a character may spend AP to perform appropriate non-attacking actions, allowing them to react to changes on the battlefield rather than waiting passively for their next turn.

During an inactive turn, characters may move on foot or by mount, take cover, and interact with the world. Firearm attacks can only be made during a character's own active turn.

Actions

Actions such as talking or activating Parley do not require AP. Keep in mind that the enemy may not care about your efforts at negotiation.

Actions that do require AP are usually performed during combat. These include movement, shooting, reloading, taking cover, sneaking, mounting or dismounting a horse, lassoing, and world interactions. Actions that require AP are not limited to combat; your GM may require AP during tense moments, puzzles, chases, and other situations.

Firearms

Hit Rolls and Location Rolls

Firearm attacks use two separate d20 rolls: a Hit Roll and a Location Roll. The Hit Roll determines whether your attack hits the target. If the Hit Roll succeeds, roll for the Location Roll to determine which body part is struck. If the Hit Roll fails, do not make a Location Roll.

Hit Roll Modifier

Calculate your Hit Roll modifier by subtracting 2 from your Agility modifier. Apply the resulting modifier to your Hit Roll: add it if positive or subtract it if negative. For example, an Agility modifier of +5 gives you a +3 Hit Roll modifier, while an Agility modifier of 0 gives you a -2 Hit Roll modifier.

Firing

Firing a firearm costs 1 Action Point (AP), regardless of whether the attack hits or misses.

Reloading

Reloading costs vary depending on the firearm. Consult WEAPONS AND ITEMS to find the specific AP cost required to reload your weapon.

Hit Location

To successfully hit a target with a firearm, your Hit Roll must meet or exceed the target's Defense Bonus (DB). The DB functions similarly to Armor Class (AC) in Dungeons & Dragons: it is the number you must roll on your d20 to successfully hit the target. If your Hit Roll equals or exceeds the target's DB, the attack hits, and you roll for hit location. If your Hit Roll is lower than the target's DB, the attack misses.

RollLocationEffect
1HeadThe target is killed instantly, no matter the DB.
2–5ArmsThe target drops whatever they are holding and makes a DC 9 Condition Check. On a failure, the arm is incapacitated and cannot be used. On a success, the arm remains functional.
6–9LegsThe target makes a DC 9 Condition Check. On a failure, the leg is incapacitated and the target's movement speed is halved. On a success, the leg remains functional and movement is unaffected.
10–20TorsoRoll the weapon's damage normally.

The hit-location system is divided by function: the head is lethal, the torso deals damage, the arms impair utility, and the legs impair mobility.

Targeted Shots

A character may declare a Targeted Shot before firing in order to attempt to hit a specific body part. A Targeted Shot only succeeds if the Hit Roll is a natural 20. If the Hit Roll is anything other than a natural 20, the shot fails and no Location Roll is made.

Targeted Shots cannot be declared while the character is riding a horse.

Mounts and Firearms

When firing a firearm while riding a horse, the attack is made with disadvantage.

A character riding a horse cannot declare a Targeted Shot. Mounted firearm attacks therefore rely on the normal Hit Roll and Location Roll system.

Condition Checks

The standard Condition Check difficulty is DC 5. Firearm injuries to the arms and legs specifically use DC 9.

For firearm injuries to the arms and legs, the Condition Check determines whether the injury causes its associated impairment. A successful check means the associated impairment does not occur.

Knives

Knives are primarily close-range weapons that provide an alternative to firearms. They are not intended to compete with firearms in raw damage, but instead offer a simple and versatile option for characters who choose not to rely on guns. Knives can also be useful for characters seeking a quieter way to eliminate an opponent when circumstances allow. Their primary combat utility is Release, which allows a character equipped with a knife to attempt to escape a grapple. Beyond this, knives remain relatively simple weapons, relying on close-range attacks rather than numerous specialized mechanics.

Knife attacks use the same Hit Roll system as firearms. If the Hit Roll succeeds, the attacker rolls a Location Roll to determine where the strike lands. The effects of the strike depend on the location rolled and the type of attack being performed.

Knife Hit Locations

RollLocationEffect
1–7 (35%)ArmsThe target drops whatever they are holding and makes a DC 9 Condition Check. On a failure, the struck arm is incapacitated and cannot be used. On a success, the arm remains functional.
8–14 (35%)LegsThe target makes a DC 5 Condition Check. On a failure, the struck leg is incapacitated and the target's movement speed is halved. On a success, the leg remains functional and movement is unaffected.
15–20 (30%)TorsoApply damage according to the type of knife attack being performed.

Slashing

Slashing deals an initial 1d4 damage and inflicts the Bleeding condition when it hits the torso. While the target is bleeding, they take an additional 1d4 damage at the start of each of their active turns until the wound is bandaged. This bleeding effect only applies to torso hits.

Stabbing

Stabbing deals greater initial damage of 1d6 but causes little to no recurring bleeding. Stabbing attacks only deal their damage when the Location Roll indicates a torso hit. If the roll indicates the arms or legs, the stabbing attack does not connect with the torso, and its normal stabbing damage is not applied. The Condition DC roll for stabbing attacks is DC 14.

Slit Throat

Knives also have a special action called Slit Throat. When sneaking behind someone, a character may declare that they are attempting to slit the target's throat. This action succeeds only on a natural 20 on the Hit Roll and serves as the knife equivalent of a firearm headshot. The action can be heard by anyone within a 10-foot radius. Because this is a declared action, the attacker must announce their intention to attempt it before rolling.

Release

Knives also have a Release function that allows a character to cut themselves free from a lasso without spending AP. Instead of spending 3 AP to untangle themselves, a character equipped with a knife can attempt to cut the lasso and escape by succeeding on a DC 5 Condition Check. This action costs no AP.

Grappling

Grappling is divided into two types: Physical Grappling and Lasso Grappling.

Physical Grappling

A Physical Grapple represents directly controlling another character, such as tackling them or restraining their arms. To initiate a Physical Grapple, the attacker makes a Might Check against the target's Might, with a DC equal to the target's Might. If the attacker succeeds, the target becomes physically grappled.

To escape a Physical Grapple, compare the Might of both characters. If the grappled character has higher Might than the grappler, they automatically overcome the grapple. If their Might is equal to or lower than the grappler's, they must succeed on a DC 10 Might Check to escape.

Lasso Grappling

A Lasso Grapple costs 2 AP and requires a Hit Roll against the target's DB. If the Hit Roll succeeds, both characters roll a d20 and add their Agility modifier. If the attacker's total is higher, the target becomes Lassoed. A Lassoed character cannot move freely.

A lassoed individual may use Release if they have a knife equipped, cutting the lasso and escaping. Without an equipped knife, they must spend 3 AP and succeed on a Might Check against DC 15 to escape. The attacker may spend 1 AP to pull the target 5 feet closer. The attacker does not need to physically hold the target to maintain the lasso.

Punching and Physical Attacks

Punching or making any other unarmed physical attack requires you to be within 5 feet of your opponent. To determine whether an attack hits, roll against the target's Defense Class (DC) divided by 2. Unarmed damage is calculated by dividing your Might score by the result of a 1d6 roll. Making one punch costs 1 Action Point (AP), and each punch requires its own attack roll and damage roll.

Cover

Cover in Dust & Blood works a little differently than in most tabletop RPGs. Cover protects specific parts of a character's body rather than making them harder to hit overall.

When attacking an enemy behind cover, roll your Hit Roll normally. If the attack hits, roll for the Hit Location as usual. If the body part you rolled is protected by cover, the shot hits the cover instead, and the target takes no damage. If the body part is exposed, the attack hits the target normally.

Gun Handling

Every gun has a minimum required number of hands to use the weapon. Some traits will alter this; consult the weapon-type tables. For example, if you need two hands to use a weapon but want to climb a ladder or lead a horse, you cannot use that weapon while doing so.

When you go prone and mount your weapon against the ground, or mount it on a stable surface such as a windowsill, you gain +5 to Hit. This only works with rifles.

Helping Hand

When a character assists an ally with an Ability Check, the assisting character rolls 4d6. Convert the total rolled into its corresponding modifier using the same rules as character creation. Apply that modifier to the ally's Ability Check, adding it if positive or subtracting it if negative. A high roll can improve the ally's chances of success, while a low roll can hinder them.

Proficiency in Weapons

If you train in a weapon during downtime, or gain more than 100 XP with the weapon, you gain proficiency with it. You add your proficiency bonus to the Hit Roll.

Gun Modifications

Every firearm has three modification slots that can be filled with different gun modifications to improve its performance. Modifications grant specific mechanical bonuses, such as reducing Action Point (AP) costs, improving accuracy, increasing ammunition capacity, or improving reload speed. Modifications can be interchanged during downtime, allowing players to customize their firearms to suit their playstyle. Each modification provides a distinct benefit, giving players the freedom to build their weapons around their preferred approach to combat.

Weapon Type Tables

The following tables describe weapon types, their required hands, and their mechanical effects.

Handguns

Single-Action Revolver1Grants +1 to Hit Rolls when the hammer is cocked before firing. Cocking the hammer costs 1 AP.
Double-Action Revolver1Can fire without manually cocking the hammer. No additional AP cost to cock.

pages.title: Outdoor Activities
pages.body:
Outdoor Activities

Fishing

Fishing in Dust & Blood is resolved using three dice rolls. First, the player rolls a d20 to beat the Fishing DC assigned to the lake. The roll must be higher than the DC to successfully catch a fish; otherwise, the attempt fails. On a successful fishing check, the player rolls another d20 on the Freshwater Fish Table to determine which species they catch. The player then rolls a d12 on the Fish Size Table to determine the fish's size, ranging from tiny to trophy-sized. The fish's size determines its final selling price by multiplying its base price by the appropriate size modifier. The GM determines the fish's actual length and weight based on its species and size category.

Fish Size Table

After determining the fish species, roll a d12 to determine its size. Apply the result to the fish's normal size range.

D12 RollSize CategorySize DescriptionSelling Price Modifier
1Tiny50% of normal minimum size×0.25

Fishing Rules

Requirement: You must have a fishing pole with bait or a lure.

  1. Roll a d20 against the lake's Fishing DC. You must roll higher than the DC to catch a fish.
  2. If successful, roll a d20 on the Freshwater Fish Table.
  3. Roll a d12 on the Fish Size Table to determine the fish's size category.
  4. Multiply the fish's base selling price by its size modifier to determine its final value.
  5. The GM determines the fish's actual length and weight based on its species and size category.

Example: You fish in a lake with a Fishing DC of 10 and roll a 15. You then roll a 9 on the Freshwater Fish Table, catching a Brown Trout. Your d12 size roll is 10, making it Very Large. Its base price of $0.45 is multiplied by 2, making it worth $0.90.

Foraging

Foraging in Dust & Blood is resolved through three dice rolls. First, the player rolls a d20 to beat the Foraging DC assigned to the forest. The roll must exceed the DC to successfully find a plant; otherwise, the attempt fails. On a successful foraging check, the player rolls a d20 on the Plant Species Table to determine which herb they discover. Once the plant species has been determined, the player rolls a d4 on the Plant Purity Table to establish the purity of the herb they have gathered.
